edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. XII, printed pp. 6-8 (PDF pp. 30-32)

source_text: Si quis dixerit, Christum sola opinione atque fictitie apparuisse mundo; et non confessus fuerit ipsum in carne venisse; anathema sit. Quomodo potest quispiam dicere, Christum putatitie ac ficte apparuisse mundo; Christum dico, in Bethleem natum, ad circumcisionem carnis adductum, a Symeone gestatum; usque ad duodecimum annum a parentibus educatum, iisque morigerum; in Iordane baptizatum, in cruce confixum, et a mortuis suscitatum? Quamobrem dum dicitur: Turbatus est spiritu, tristatus est anima, vulneratus est corpore; appellationes passionum secundum naturae nostrae constitutionem asserit, ut ostendat se hominem in mundo esse natum, et cum hominibus conversatum ad similitudinem nostram, sine tamen peccato. Natus est enim in Bethleem secundum carnem, ut Deum decebat, Angelis caelestibus Dominum suum agnoscentibus, et Deum in praesepio pannis involutum collaudantibus, atque dicentibus: Gloria in altissimis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis. In Nazaret enutritus est. In medio Doctorum sedens, Deum se ostendit, et admirationem eis movit super sapientia praeter tempus aetatis, secundum corpus, sicut Evangelicus sermo enarrat. In Iordane baptizatus est, non ut sanctificationem assumeret, sed ut sanctificationis participationem aliis elargiretur. In deserto tentatus est, non subiectus tentationi: sed nostras tentationes provocationi tentatoris obiiciens; ut vanum esse tentantem demonstraret. Propterea ait: Confidite, ego vici mundum. Non divinam luctationem opponens; sed propriam carnem victricem passionis, et mortis, atque corruptionis ostendens: ut per quam carnem, peccatum intravit in mundum, et per peccatum mors in omnibus hominibus regnavit; per eandem carnem secundum similitudinem, damnaretur peccatum in carne; et vinceretur peccati praeses qui tentat; et mors dissolveretur, ne regnaret; et corruptio in corporis sepultura evanesceret; primitiaeque resurrectionis ostenderentur, et principium iustitiae in mundo per fidem exerceretur; regnumque caelorum hominibus adnunciaretur, et Dei cum hominibus communio iniretur. Pro hac gratia glorificemus patrem, qui dedit filium suum unigenitum pro mundi vita: glorificemus spiritum sanctum, qui operatur in nobis et vivificat nos, et charismata ad communionem cum Deo ineundam tribuit: et ne doctrinam Evangelicam curiose verbis aridis perscrutemur, interminatas quaestiones et pugnas verborum circunferentes; et planum ac facilem, rectumque de fide sermonem, asperum reddentes: sed potius operemur opus fidei, pacem amemus, concordiam praeferamus, unitatem atque coniunctionem servemus, charitatem excolamus, per quam placatur Deus. Quemadmodum autem nostrum non est, scire tempora aut momenta quae pater posuit in sua potestate; credere autem oportet, finem fore huius temporis, et futuram venturi saeculi manifestationem, ac iudicii revelationem, et filii Dei adventum, operumque retributionem, ac hereditatis regni caelorum possessionem: sic non est nostrum scire, quomodo filius Dei factus sit homo. Mysterium enim hoc magnum est, sicut scriptum est, Generationem eius quis enarrabit? quia tollitur de terra vita eius. Sed credere oportet, quod filius Dei factus sit homo secundum Scripturas; et quod in terra visus sit, et cum hominibus conversatus, ut scripturae docent, ad similitudinem nostram, absque peccato; quodque pro nobis mortuus sit, et resurrexit ex mortuis, sicut scriptum est; et quod in caelos assumptus sit, sedetque in dextera patris, unde venturus est iudicare vivos et mortuos, sicut Scriptura docet: ne forte dum verbis inter nos contendimus, blasphement quidam doctrinam fidei; eveniatque quod dictum est: Propter vos semper blasphematur nomen meum in gentibus.
thought_title: Christ came truly in the flesh, not in appearance only
orientation: Gregory condemns the view that Christ appeared only in seeming, retells the true events of his life in the flesh, and closes the work with praise of the Trinity and a warning against quarrels over words.
pass_a_gloss: If anyone shall have said Christ appeared (apparuisse) to the world by opinion alone (sola opinione) and fictitiously (fictitie); and shall not have confessed him to have come in the flesh (in carne venisse); let him be anathema. How can anyone say Christ appeared to the world putatively (putatitie) and feignedly (ficte); Christ, I say, born in Bethlehem, brought to circumcision of the flesh (circumcisionem carnis), carried (gestatum) by Symeon; until the twelfth year brought up by parents, and obedient (morigerum) to them; baptized in the Jordan, fixed to the cross (in cruce confixum), and raised (suscitatum) from the dead? Wherefore while it is said: He was troubled (turbatus) in spirit, saddened (tristatus) in soul, wounded (vulneratus) in body; he asserts (asserit) the names of passions (appellationes passionum) according to the constitution (constitutionem) of our nature, that he may show himself born man in the world, and having lived (conversatum) with men to our likeness (similitudinem), yet without sin (sine peccato). For he was born in Bethlehem according to the flesh, as befitted God (ut Deum decebat), the heavenly Angels acknowledging (agnoscentibus) their Lord, and praising (collaudantibus) God wrapped in cloths (pannis involutum) in the manger (praesepio), and saying: Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace to men of good will (bonae voluntatis). In Nazareth he was nourished (enutritus). Sitting in the midst of the Teachers (Doctorum), he showed himself God, and moved admiration in them over wisdom beyond the time of age, according to the body, as the Gospel word (Evangelicus sermo) narrates. In the Jordan he was baptized, not that he might assume sanctification (sanctificationem), but that he might bestow (elargiretur) on others participation (participationem) of sanctification. In the desert he was tempted (tentatus), not subject (subiectus) to temptation: but throwing against (obiiciens) our temptations to the provocation (provocationi) of the tempter; that he might demonstrate the tempting one to be vain (vanum). Therefore he says: Be confident (confidite), I have conquered (vici) the world. Not opposing a divine wrestling (luctationem); but showing his own flesh victorious (victricem) of passion, and of death, and of corruption: that through which flesh sin entered into the world, and through sin death reigned in all men; through the same flesh according to likeness, sin might be condemned (damnaretur) in the flesh; and the ruler (praeses) of sin who tempts might be conquered; and death might be dissolved (dissolveretur), lest it reign; and corruption might vanish (evanesceret) in the burial (sepultura) of the body; and the first fruits (primitiae) of the resurrection might be shown, and the beginning (principium) of righteousness (iustitiae) in the world through faith might be exercised; and the kingdom of the heavens might be announced to men, and the communion (communio) of God with men might be entered (iniretur). For this grace (gratia) let us glorify the father, who gave his only-begotten (unigenitum) son for the life of the world: let us glorify the holy spirit, who works (operatur) in us and gives us life (vivificat), and bestows gifts (charismata) for entering communion with God: and let us not curiously (curiose) search out (perscrutemur) the Gospel teaching (doctrinam) with dry words, carrying around (circunferentes) unlimited questions (interminatas quaestiones) and fights of words (pugnas verborum); and rendering rough (asperum) the plain and easy and right word (sermonem) about faith: but rather let us work the work of faith (opus fidei), let us love peace, prefer concord (concordiam), keep unity and conjunction (coniunctionem), cultivate charity (charitatem), through which God is appeased (placatur). But as it is not ours to know times or moments which the father has placed in his own power (potestate); but it is necessary to believe there will be an end of this time, and a future manifestation (manifestationem) of the age to come, and revelation of judgment, and coming (adventum) of the son of God, and retribution (retributionem) of works, and possession of the inheritance (hereditatis) of the kingdom of the heavens: so it is not ours to know how the son of God was made man. For this mystery (mysterium) is great, as it is written, His generation (generationem) who will narrate? because his life is taken from the earth. But it is necessary to believe that the son of God was made man according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen on earth, and lived with men, as the scriptures teach, to our likeness, without sin; and that he died for us, and rose from the dead, as it is written; and that he was taken up (assumptus) into the heavens, and sits at the right hand of the father, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture teaches: lest perhaps (ne forte) while we contend (contendimus) with words among ourselves, some blaspheme (blasphement) the teaching of the faith; and there come to pass what was said: Because of you my name is always (semper) blasphemed among the nations (gentibus).

pass_b_english: If anyone says that Christ appeared to the world only in seeming and pretense, and does not confess that he came in the flesh (1 John 4:2), let him be anathema.

How can anyone say that Christ appeared to the world in seeming and pretense? I mean Christ, born in Bethlehem; brought to be circumcised in the flesh (Luke 2:21); carried by Simeon (Luke 2:28); brought up by his parents until his twelfth year and obedient to them (Luke 2:42; Luke 2:51); baptized in the Jordan, nailed to the cross, and raised from the dead? Therefore, when it is said, “He was troubled in spirit” (John 13:21), “He was grieved in soul” (Matthew 26:38), “He was wounded in body,” he claims the names of these sufferings in keeping with the make-up of our nature, to show that he was born a man in the world and lived among men in our likeness, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

For he was born in Bethlehem according to the flesh, as befitted God, while the heavenly angels recognized their Lord and praised God wrapped in swaddling cloths in the manger (Luke 2:7), saying, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2:14). He was brought up in Nazareth. Sitting in the midst of the teachers, he showed himself to be God and moved them to wonder at his wisdom, which went beyond the age of his body, as the Gospel account relates (Luke 2:46–47). He was baptized in the Jordan (Matthew 3:13–16), not to receive sanctification, but to bestow on others a share in sanctification. He was tempted in the desert (Matthew 4:1), not as one subject to temptation, but setting our temptations against the challenge of the tempter, to show the tempter to be futile.

That is why he says, “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). He did not put forward a divine struggle, but showed his own flesh victorious over suffering, death and corruption, so that through the very flesh by which sin entered into the world, and through sin death reigned in all men (Romans 5:12–14), through that same flesh, in its likeness, sin might be condemned in the flesh (Romans 8:3); the ruler of sin, the tempter, might be overcome; death might be undone, so that it would not reign; corruption might vanish in the burial of the body; the first fruits of the resurrection might be shown; the beginning of righteousness might be set to work in the world through faith; the kingdom of heaven might be proclaimed to men; and communion between God and men might be entered into.

For this grace let us glorify the Father, who gave his only-begotten Son (John 3:16) for the life of the world (John 6:51). Let us glorify the Holy Spirit, who works in us and gives us life, and grants the gifts of grace for entering into communion with God. And let us not pry with curiosity and dry words into the teaching of the Gospel, bandying about endless questions (1 Timothy 1:4) and battles of words (1 Timothy 6:4), and making rough the plain, easy and straight word about the faith. Rather, let us do the work of faith, love peace, put concord first, keep unity and fellowship, and cultivate love, by which God is appeased.

It is not for us to know the times or seasons which the Father has set in his own authority (Acts 1:7); but we must believe that there will be an end of this present time, and the manifestation of the age to come, the revelation of the judgment, the coming of the Son of God, the repayment of works, and the possession of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. In the same way, it is not for us to know how the Son of God became man. For this mystery is great, as it is written: “Who will declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth” (Isaiah 53:8).

But we must believe that the Son of God became man according to the Scriptures; that he was seen on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3:38), as the Scriptures teach, in our likeness, without sin; that he died for us and rose from the dead, as it is written (1 Corinthians 15:3–4); and that he was taken up into the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father (Mark 16:19), from where he will come to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1), as Scripture teaches. Otherwise, while we contend with one another in words, some may blaspheme the teaching of the faith, and what was said may come to pass: “Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Isaiah 52:5).
notes: Sola opinione atque fictitie / putatitie ac ficte rendered “seeming and pretense” (the Docetic view).
The edition prints no separate closing heading: the doxology and the closing exhortation belong to Interpretatio XII, and the row is kept as one section in seven paragraphs.
The print repeats Deus across a line break before Quemadmodum; the dittography is dropped (facing Greek has Theos once).

“He was wounded in body” has no single verse (perhaps Isaiah 53:5, vulneratus est) and is left uncited; the first two clauses match John 13:21 (turbatus est spiritu) and Matthew 26:38 (tristis est anima mea).
Margin at Deum se ostendit has Greek theoprepos (“in a manner befitting God”); the Latin reading “showed himself to be God” is kept.
Asserit (“he claims”) takes Christ as subject, as ut ostendat se hominem requires.
Obiiciens provocationi rendered “setting … against the challenge”; vanum “futile”.
Secundum similitudinem rendered “in its likeness”, an echo of Romans 8:3 (in similitudinem carnis peccati).

Primitiae resurrectionis may echo 1 Corinthians 15:20, 23, opus fidei 1 Thessalonians 1:3, the Spirit who gives life John 6:63, the mystery being great 1 Timothy 3:16 or Ephesians 5:32, and blaspheming the teaching 1 Timothy 6:1 or Titus 2:5; all are left uncited as uncertain.
Interminatas quaestiones follows 1 Timothy 1:4 (genealogiis interminatis, quae quaestiones praestant); at circunferentes a marginal gloss is too blurred to read.
The second “in our likeness, without sin” is not cited again (Hebrews 4:15 given above).
At in caelos assumptus sit the margin has al. ascendit; text kept, cited to Mark 16:19 (assumptus est in caelum, et sedet a dextris Dei).
“Judge the living and the dead” also stands in Acts 10:42 and 1 Peter 4:5.

The last quotation follows Isaiah 52:5 in its LXX form (“because of you … continually … among the Gentiles”), which Romans 2:24 also quotes; at nomen meum the margin has al. nomen Dei (partly obscured), which is the form of Romans 2:24; text kept.
The editor's margin sigla on pp. 6–8 were read only at scan resolution; each citation here was checked from the wording.
